questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
As a Japanese Studies student, it was crucial that my destination was in Japan, and with my hopes of constructing lasting relationships with not only locals and international students, but also with companies and individuals with connections within a professional area, a central location near Tokyo was preferred, and was one of the reasons for picking this destination.

Aside from this, I knew that Meiji had a faint connection with the Nordics, and this fit with my previous exchange destinations within Japan. Finally, I felt that the courses and level of education that the selected university was capable of delivering was satisfactory to my needs, and in most cases, this proved to be true.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
I had no issues upon arrival, even despite arriving earlier than most other exchange students, as well as living in my own, seperately arranged accomodation. Mails were sent to aid us in what documents, etc. was required, and aside from this, the staff at Nakano Ward Office were extremely helpful in guiding me.

It should be mentioned that I am fluent in Japanese, and had already exchanged once, so I was aware of the move-in procedures as well as the documents required for this.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Because I was able to travel over one month before the start of classes, I didn't have much in the way of guidance for the first weeks. There was no physical contact with any staff of the university until after the start of classes.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I had no issues with the level of assistance at this university, although I did feel their presence was relatively small. I did not live in the dormitories like the majority of the students did, so I am unsure of the process from their side.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
If you're not looking for a Share House, which can sometimes be a lottery in terms of cleanliness, privacy, etc., then it's apt to budget around 80-120.000 JPY for rent a month. I was able to find an older rental through Fontana City Apartments, who were helpful and honest throughout the whole process from my perspective. The price and state of the apartment was subpar for the area, but Fontana offered short-term rentals and relatively few fees, so it was the lesser of two evils.

My apartment was within walking distance of the university (under 30 minutes) and close to public transport (Marunouchi Line's Shin-Nakano stop).

Most apartments in Japan require a large sum of key-money, a deposit which is not likely to be returned as well as a minimum contract length of two years. For most one semester exchange progrmas, it is not possible to rent an apartment without incurring significant costs - if they will even allow you to rent.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
As far as I know, most of the dormitories were far away, and the lottery system didn't consider main faculty when distributing the students, so some had almost an hour of commuting. Still, relatively few choose to live in seperate accomodations closer to the campus, so the student life is somewhat lonely without local friends - and even then, few live close to campus.

With this in mind, I would recommend staying in one of the dorms.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: After a week of being able to trial classes, we could decide on our classes through an online system. Despite missing a class in this first week, it was still possible to follow it, and also to change classes last-minute. I had no issues.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Plenty of introductory sessions helped prepare for selecting classes, and any professor was helpful in giving advice.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: A few of the classes were lottery-classes with limited numbers for international students. I was picked for all my first-priority classes, so I never paid it any mind.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try as many classes as you can, and don't plan any events in the first weeks. There are some online classes which can't be trialled, and I would seriously consider leaving those behind if I was to exchange again.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Courses were BA-level, and half of my credits were for elective classes, while another half was dedicated to Realia B.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Generally, online and on-demand courses were more prevalent at Meiji University, and I think this ties in with the general style of teaching at Japanese universities. There were fewer long assignments, and professors instead focused on having you submit a small pages worth of notes from each lesson. For the final submissions, which were the only large submission for most classes, a proper page requirement was usually set, although it felt at times like the contents of this paper were largely irrelevant to the final mark. Particularly sources and source creditation seemed to be of less importance, perhaps due to the diverse background of the students present - some had not learned the conventions at the time of exchange, while others had. In any case, a higher level of strictness and adherence to rules was generally displayed by foreign professors, while local, Japanese professors seemed less inclined to care.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Animation Culture
Manga Culture
Japan and technology
Japanese Social Systems
Journalism Studies
Media Studies
Production Management

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
While the Manga and Anime Culture classes may seem like free-time fun at a glance, the professor is not only extremely knowledgeable and a good presenter, but also seems to care about the products and opinions of each student. I recommend these classes.

For anyone with an interest in Japan and Japanese society, Japanese Social Systems gave a good rundown of modern Japanese political and economical issues, and allowed time and space to ponder these.

I don't recommend Journalism Studies and Media Studies - these were online courses, were eerily similar, and didn't have a particularly deep level of engagement. The Journalism Course was non-timed and entirely on-demand, which meant I could complete it in the month of exam preparation and in-between classes.

The Production Management and Japan and Technology classes were average, with some interesting and useful points, and other somewhat redundant points.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It may come as a surprise to some, that health insurance is required despite paying from home. A monthly payment of around 1.700 JPY is required for the Japanese Government, while a one-time payment for Meiji University is required for other insurance coverages.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Inflation has hit hard in Japan, so living costs, but particularly foods, are more expensive now than they were last time I was there. When I attemped to live frugally, it was not an issue, but my spending habits during the first couple of months did provide some surprises and wide-eyed looks at my bank statements.

Also, Meiji allows exchange students to qualify for student discounts on things like Shinkansen-tickets, so make sure to take advantage of this while away. This should also be explained in the introduction.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Many clubs (called saakuru in Japanese universities) were advertised, and apparently, they were welcoming to foreigners. Most, however, were located at differnet campuses, and most of my peers were never enrolled in any of these.

Some student events were dotted around the calendar, but I found it odd that these were usually heavily limited, and required good relationship with your local kami of luck. The most surprising case of this, was when a cultural exchange event only allowed 5 (!!!) exchange students to attend, despite having space for loads more.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Halloween events, cultural exchange events and a Christmas party was arranged. Most actual events were paid, while I think the clubs were free. There was an indoor ball-games court at my campus in Nakano, which was apparently free to use. I never did.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I liked the Christmas party, but mostly, I would recommend making some friends at the dorm and asking them to be invited over every now and then.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
There's plenty to do in Tokyo, but I often found myself just making a nice dinner at home. Raw ingredients are cheaper and different compared to Denmark, especially fish, so I recommend trying as much as you can.

Tokyo is central enough that you can pretty much travel anywhere easily by Shinkansen - if not, most domestic flights leave from Haneda, which is super close to both the dorms and the university. I recommend Tohoku in winter.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think Danish and Japanese people have a similar respect for public order and quiet, although it is more enforced in Japan, so be aware of things like talking on the phone in the train, getting drunk and rowdy with your friends, or the like.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: This was my biggest issue with Meiji University - there were few points where you could naturally talk to local students. There's a Study Cafe in the bottom floor of the Nakano Campus, though, and the local students that come here are usually talkative and extroverted.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Many describe Japanese as being part-time friends, with meeting once a month or so being enough. This was difficult, because as an exchange student, you only have 6 months at max. I recommend keeping a mix of international and local friends to avoid getting left alone.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Definitely the order. Later in my exchange, I was able to visit Shanghai and Wuhu in China, and the chaos there reminded me just how calm and ordered Japan is. Just be aware that this can also backfire, when you're trying to go around the rules.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1: Get a dorm. An apartment is not worth it.
2: Don't waste your time just in Tokyo. Spend some cash and go see Japan.
3: In a good way, don't take your classes to seriously. You'll stress to keep up with it all, and won't have time to enjoy the local culture.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: You're not required to pay towards your national pension when you're just an exchange student making no money. If you ever receive the payment slips in the mail (they're alot more expensive than the health insurance, so you'll know), don't pay them, and take them, along with your student card, to the Ward Office. They'll sort it out for you.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I have an interest in cars, and getting to meet and engage with people from Nissan and Toyota was a very rewarding experience.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Fighting enourmous cockroaches in the middle of the night in my cheapo apartment in Tokyo. Don't do it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
